If Tesla and SpaceX merged, Elon Musk could oversee a single company holding about 30,221 Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), valued at about $1.81 billion. This follows Musk's comments during SpaceX's earnings call on October 20, 2026, where he said Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) and SpaceX have each formed special committees of independent directors to explore a merger.

While no formal terms have been announced, both companies hold Bitcoin, which has fallen 29.8% this year. So, how much Bitcoin would a merged company control, and what could be done with those assets?

Loren Elliott/Getty Images
Tesla and SpaceX Could Combine to Hold $1.81 Billion in Bitcoin
PalSand / Shutterstock.com

Tesla holds 11,509 Bitcoin, while SpaceX owns 18,712, combining for a total of 30,221 coins, according to CoinGecko's treasury tracker. With Bitcoin trading at about $59,891. Tesla's holdings are worth about $689 million, and SpaceX's are valued at about $1.12 billion, for a total of roughly $1.81 billion.

This joint holding would make the merged company the fifth-largest public firm by Bitcoin holdings. However, it is still a fraction of the leader, Strategy (NASDAQ: MSTR), which holds 851,305 Bitcoin—over 28 times as much. title: RBC Expects SpaceX-Tesla Deal Announcement By Early 2027 — Notes TSLA Shareholders May Accept Combination Without Large Premium

RBC Expects SpaceX-Tesla Deal Announcement By Early 2027 — Notes TSLA Shareholders May Accept Combination Without Large Premium
Anan Ashraf
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 4:55 PM EST 4 min read
TSLA
SPCX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The Financial Times reported on Tuesday that Tesla and SpaceX have appointed five directors to guide a merger deal.

Gary Black opined that a deal giving a 25% premium for Tesla would imply substantial dilution to SpaceX shares and create the largest merger in corporate history.

According to an ongoing Stocktwits poll, 45% of about 1,700 respondents believe a SpaceX-Tesla deal will be announced by year-end.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Ken Herbert said on Tuesday that he expects a deal announcement between EV giant Tesla Inc. and rocket company SpaceX by early 2027, earlier than it previously expected.

Herbert noted that a premium to Tesla's intrinsic value could be justified, though investor feedback suggests Tesla shareholders may accept a combination without a large premium. RBC maintains 'Outperform' ratings on both stocks.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

The comment comes on the heels of a report from The Financial Times that the two companies have appointed five directors to guide a merger deal. As per the report, the five directors are Roelof Botha and Randy Glein from SpaceX and Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, and Jack Hartung from Tesla. The committees are supported by advisers including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs for SpaceX and Evercore for Tesla, which are refining financial models for a potential all-stock deal, the report said.

The report described the process as moving toward a possible year-end timeline for what could be a roughly $3.5 trillion transaction, though no terms have been agreed and a deal is not assured.

Deal Repercussions For SPCX

In a post on X, The Future Fund LLC managing partner Gary Black highlighted declines in both stocks following the report, with SpaceX down more sharply. He outlined a likely all-equity structure in which SpaceX would acquire Tesla, estimating that a 25% premium for Tesla would imply substantial dilution to SpaceX shares and create the largest merger in corporate history.

Black noted that in equity-for-equity deals, the acquirer's shares often face pressure ahead of close as investors position for a lengthy 12- to 18-month process. While TSLA stock closed flat on Tuesday, SPCX closed down 6%.

Source: Gary Black/ X

The developments follow Elon Musk's remarks on SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call, in which he confirmed that both boards had formed special committees of independent directors to discuss a potential combination at shareholders' request. Musk, who described himself as a conflicted party unable to participate in the talks, said a merger would be "a good idea" given overlapping work in AI, robotics, and related technologies, while cautioning that it was not certain and would require a high threshold of Tesla shareholder approval.

title: Tesla and SpaceX Name Five Directors for a Potential $3.5 Trillion Merger. Tesla Holders Still Get a Vote
detail:
Tesla and SpaceX Name Five Directors for a Potential $3.5 Trillion Merger. Tesla Holders Still Get a Vote
Bobby Sankhagowit
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 3:05 PM EST 4 min read
TSLA
SPCX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Tesla and SpaceX Name Five Directors for a Potential $3.5 Trillion Merger. Tesla Holders Still Get a Vote ©U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley and kb group via Canva
Key Takeaways

Tesla and SpaceX have reportedly named five directors to negotiate a potential all-stock merger of two companies worth about $3.5 trillion together.

Tesla shareholders have the most riding on the exchange ratio, because Tesla trades at about 4x SpaceX's forward earnings multiple.

Any deal needs a majority of all of Tesla's outstanding shares, and Elon Musk has said that vote may not succeed.

Tesla holders should vote against terms set on earnings rather than market value. The next marker is Tesla's Dec. 3 annual meeting.

Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) and SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) have reportedly picked the five people who will negotiate a merger between two companies worth about $3.5 trillion together.

On Tuesday the Financial Times reported that Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung sit on Tesla's special committee. Roelof Botha and Randy Glein sit on SpaceX's. The committees have reportedly hired bankers to build value models for an all-stock deal: Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs for SpaceX, and Evercore for Tesla.

From here, it's a fight over price.

Musk isn't promising a yes

At the New York Times' DealBook Summit last week, Andrew Ross Sorkin asked Musk, CEO of both companies, whether Tesla and SpaceX need to be together to scale up computing in orbit. Musk's answer: "No, you don't need them to be together, but would they be better together, right? I mean, probably yes."

Then he added a caveat: "These require shareholder votes, which may or may not succeed, at least in the case of Tesla."

He has good reason to hedge. Tesla's vote needs a majority of all its outstanding shares, so every share that doesn't vote counts against the deal. SpaceX has said its side needs Musk's own approval as its controlling shareholder, even though he has stepped back from the committees' talks. That leaves Tesla's holders with the one veto Musk doesn't control.

Tesla holders are paying with pricey stock

Analysts expect Tesla's normalized EPS to climb from $1.66 in 2025 to $2.16 in 2027 and $3.24 in 2028. That's still short of the $4.07 it earned in 2022:

Tesla (TSLA): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

The stock prices in a lot more than that. Tesla trades at 180x forward earnings, well above its three-year average of 138x:

Tesla (TSLA): forward (NTM) P/E, last 3 years (TIKR)

SpaceX trades at about 44x. Put differently, a dollar of Tesla stock carries about a quarter of the forward earnings that a dollar of SpaceX stock does.

title: Tesla and SpaceX Just Assembled Deal Teams for a $3.2 Trillion Merger. Here's What Investors Need to Know.
detail:
Tesla and SpaceX Just Assembled Deal Teams for a $3.2 Trillion Merger. Here's What Investors Need to Know.
Danny Vena, CPA, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 3:59 PM EST 6 min read
SPCX
TSLA
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Elon Musk has made no secret of the fact that he would like to have many (if not all) of the companies he runs under one roof. And the enigmatic CEO has already taken several steps to accomplish that goal. Artificial intelligence (AI) start-up xAI merged with Twitter (now called X) before the combined company was folded into Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) aka SpaceX.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

However, Musk's biggest coup would be to bring together SpaceX and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA). The long-rumored combination just took another step closer to reality. Reports emerged on Tuesday that the electric vehicle (EV) maker and rocket launch company had appointed a handful of directors to oversee the largest merger in corporate history.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

A marriage of titans

Bringing together two companies of this size will be a daunting task. SpaceX has a market cap of roughly $1.7 trillion, while Tesla's clocks in at $1.5 trillion, making the combined entity worth $3.2 trillion and placing it among the world's five most valuable companies (as of this writing).

SpaceX and Tesla have chosen five of the companies' directors to conduct merger negotiations, according to a report that first appeared in The Financial Times. The quintet of executives -- two from SpaceX and three from Tesla -- have been charged with hashing out the details for the all-stock merger, according to the report.

Roelof Botha of SpaceX: Former managing director of prominent venture capital firm Sequoia Capital. Botha spent more than two decades with Sequoia after serving as PayPal's CFO under Musk and has served on numerous boards of directors, including Unity Software, Block, and MongoDB.

Randy Glein of SpaceX: Co-founder of venture capital firm DFJ Growth. Glein is an aerospace engineer, and his firm was an early investor in SpaceX, taking a $10 million stake when the company was worth roughly $550 million. He has been a board member or observer for dozens of companies.

Robyn Denholm of Tesla: Australian chartered accountant and has been the automaker's board chair since 2018. Former tech executive at Sun Microsystems, which was acquired by Oracle, and Juniper Networks, which is now part of Hewlett Packard Enterprise.

Kathleen Wilson-Thompson of Tesla: Former executive with Kellogg Company and Walgreens. Served on numerous boards of directors, including Vulcan Materials and Ashland, and has been with Tesla since 2018.

Jack Hartung of Tesla: Former President and CFO of Chipotle after more than two decades with the company. Previous executive with McDonald's. Served on the boards of directors of Portillo's and The Honest Company and joined Tesla's board in 2025.
